newsitem.title: ZAIRE: More Rwanda refugees head home after Zaire ordeal.
newsitem.headline: More Rwanda refugees head home after Zaire ordeal.

text.p: More than 2,000 Rwandan refugees came out of the hills of the Masisi region into the town of Sake on Tuesday, telling of attacks by local tribesmen.

Aid workers distributed high-energy biscuits to the refugees as they lined the road on the outskirts of the tiny town, 20 kms (12 miles) west of Goma. The refugees had fled the camp of Katale in eastern Zaire over a month ago.

The refugees arriving in Sake said there were many more behind them, and aid agencies believe the latest influx could herald a second wave of refugees going home to Rwanda, following the estimated 600,000 who have returned since November 15.
The road to Sake was opened to foreign aid workers and journalists on Tuesday for the first time in days after being closed by the Zairean rebels who control the area.

"It took me a long time," said a one-legged man wearing cut-off jeans and a Frank Zappa t-shirt, propping his stump on his crutch as he nibbled at a biscuit. "You know, the roads of the Masisi were not made for those like me."
The smell of rotting bodies blew over the queue, as people edged their way towards waiting trucks.
In a hole in the volcanic rock 20 metres (yards) from the road lay the naked, decomposing corpse of a man.
His arms had been tied with rope and one had been cut off at some point in the fighting and reprisals of the past month.
The hacked-off limb lay next to the corpse.
Refugees arriving in Goma said there were "many thousands" behind them coming out of the Masisi, and other groups were said to be heading north from Bukavu, to the south of Lake Kivu.
The refugees fled the camps to escape fighting between the Zairean army, Zairean rebels and Rwandan Hutu extremists.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimated there were 1.2 million Rwandan refugees in the camps in eastern Zaire until mid-November.
The Rwandan government has said there are no genuine refugees left in Zaire, and that there is no need for a planned multinational intervention force to help the aid effort.
Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said in Goma on Monday that UNHCR and independent aid agencies were exaggerating the number of Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire to make money.
There was a problem of "hunger and famine" in Zaire, he said, but it was Zaireans caught up in the fighting who needed help, and the aid agencies should bring in food for them.

Western and African military officials who met in Stuttgart over the weekend agreed on various options to help feed the Rwandan refugees in Zaire but enthusiasm for the intervention force has waned since the refugees started flooding home.

Many of the refugees arriving in Sake had been walking for over a month since attacks by rebel Zaireans on the three refugee camps of Katale, Kahindo and Kibumba north of Goma, which had been home to over 700,000 refugees.
"I left Katale on the 31st of October," said Isaac Ndahayo, a farmer from Ruhengeri prefecture in Rwanda.
"I walked all the way to Kichanga, then towards the Masisi. On the way back to Sake we were attacked by the Mai Mai, who carried guns and spears," he said.
The Mai Mai are ethnic Zairean tribesmen who practise witchcraft and are hostile to both Hutus and Tutsis.

Ndahayo said that the column of returning refugees stretched beyond a small village more than 10 kilometres (six miles) west of Sake. "The road behind us is full of people coming down to Sake, and then to Rwanda."
Other refugees reported fighting in the Masisi between rebel Zaireans and Hutus from the former Rwandan army and militias.
At a Red Cross way-station nine kms (five miles) towards Goma, refugees from Katale who had walked through the Virunga national park told how their menfolk had been killed en route.
"Most of us are widows here," said one young woman breastfeeding a child, who asked not to give her name.
"On the way through the forest we were attacked by men in civilian clothes, carrying guns, who killed all the men. They were speaking Kinyarwanda," she said.
It was not clear whether the attackers were Zairean rebels or soldiers of the current Rwandan army disguised as rebels, hunting down fleeing Hutu Interahamwe militiamen.
